papers.title: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (per arXiv comment)
papers.tldr: In reasoning VLAs, visual perturbations can change the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical, because the most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to text-loss gradients. TNAS-guided attacks induce new collisions under identical rationales in 52.6% of 154 Alpamayo scenes (35.1% with a localized patch).
summary: Reasoning vision-language-action models expose a natural-language rationale alongside the control action so supervisors can monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible textual evidence, so an unchanged rationale has been treated as a safety signal.

At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo (driving) and InstructVLA (manipulation), the authors introduce a text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic: the locally most action-sensitive residual direction has only 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap with active text-loss gradients. They then steer visual perturbations along that direction and compare against text-gradient and unguided action attacks across 154 obstacle-annotated Alpamayo scenes and InstructVLA examples.

At matched hidden-state norms, TNAS residual interventions shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, while text-gradient moves induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. TNAS-guided attacks produce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes with full-image perturbations and 35.1% with a localized forward-camera patch, versus 4.55% for unguided action attacks; exact rationale preservation rises from 83.0% to 89.5% versus a text-preserving baseline. Takeaway: for any system that steers or monitors a shared text/action representation, checking only the text channel is insufficient—verify the action channel directly, and expect nearly orthogonal text-neutral action directions. Caveat: results are on two specific VLA stacks; the abstract does not report defensive mitigations.

papers.title: How Far Can You Steer? Behavior-Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.tldr: Frames CAA as a constrained intervention that must maximize behavioral gain under an explicit capability-loss budget (1%, 3%, 5%). Across four instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors, validation-selected effects generalize strongly to held-out data (ρ=0.945), and joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero points rises from 37.5% at 1% to 72.7% at 3%.
summary: Activation steering can move a targeted behavior while quietly degrading unrelated capabilities, so efficacy alone does not say whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition in particular lacks a standard way to bound that collateral cost.

The paper studies CAA through a behavior-capability frontier: pick interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. It evaluates four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and absolute capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5%, with control experiments that check learned behavior directions against generic activation perturbations, plus secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations.

Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize to held-out data with ρ=0.945. Joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited further gain at 5%. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer, and interventions that pass protected benchmarks can still hurt untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. Takeaway: treat steering as a constrained edit—report a capability-loss budget and the joint survival rate, not just target-behavior lift. Caveat: single-author work; absolute percentage-point budgets may not transfer across eval suites.

papers.title: When Are Two SAE Latents the Same Feature?
papers.tldr: Unifies SAE feature matching, dictionary-level discrepancy, and finite-data uncertainty through an energy-weighted optimal-transport plan under a chosen similarity geometry, with joint asymptotic confidence bands from a document bootstrap. Experiments across four language models locate cross-seed discrepancy and separate context-dependent changes.
summary: Comparing sparse autoencoders usually treats feature correspondence, whole-dictionary distance, and sampling uncertainty as separate problems, which makes it hard to say when two latents are the same feature or how stable that claim is under finite evaluation data.

The authors build an energy-weighted optimal-transport plan under a specified similarity geometry that yields a dictionary-level discrepancy, a per-latent contribution, and a mass distribution over counterparts. They characterize relationships among decoder, activation, and first-order causal similarities, use idealized models to interpret splitting and absorption, and derive joint asymptotic inference for transport costs and fractions with a joint document bootstrap for simultaneous confidence bands.

Experiments across four language models locate cross-seed discrepancy and separate context-dependent changes; the abstract gives no numeric effect sizes. Takeaway: when matching SAE features across seeds or training runs, report the transport plan, per-latent mass spread, and bootstrap confidence bands rather than a single greedy matching score. Caveat: abstract does not name the four models or quantify how often transport reassigns mass.

papers.title: From Activation to Intervention: Interpreting Sparse Visual Features through Reconstruction
papers.tldr: RecSAEI explains vision SAE features by intervening along decoder directions and reconstructing the image, which disambiguates co-activating features such as texture versus color that top-activating patches leave ambiguous. It also grounds [CLS] SAE interventions in a sparse set of patch SAE decoder directions.
summary: Sparse autoencoders decompose visual representations into features, but explaining a feature from its top-activating images or pixels is ambiguous when several features with different semantics fire in the same places, such as texture and color.

Reconstructive SAE Intervention (RecSAEI) shifts explanation from passive observation to active reconstruction: intervene on representations along SAE decoder directions and reconstruct the visual output as direct evidence of the feature's meaning. The framework is tested across multiple datasets and vision encoders, and it attributes [CLS] SAE interventions to a sparse set of patch SAE decoder directions.

The method successfully disambiguates feature meanings in the reported settings and exposes compositional links between elementary visual patterns and high-level semantics; the abstract gives no numeric metrics. Takeaway: for vision SAEs (and for medical imaging prototypes that rely on activation maps), pair top-activating evidence with intervention reconstruction so co-located features are not conflated. Caveat: abstract does not name datasets, encoders, or quantitative gains; demo and code are linked.

papers.title: Reducing Logprob Without Causal Verification: Diagnosing SAE-Based PII Suppression in LLMs
papers.source: arXiv cs.AI, accepted to Findings of AACL-IJCNLP 2026 (per arXiv comment)
papers.tldr: Log-probability drop alone cannot tell SAE feature suppression of PII from a magnitude artifact of large activation edits: of 36 (model, layer, PII type) cases, 47% look successful under logprob-only scoring but only 2.8% pass a multimetric check against coherence-matched random directions.
summary: SAE feature interventions aimed at suppressing personally identifiable information in LLMs are usually judged by how much they reduce the log-probability of PII tokens. That criterion may credit any large activation perturbation, not a feature-specific causal edit.

Across 36 (model, layer, PII type) cases the authors compare selected SAE feature interventions with coherence-matched random-direction controls using logprob and rank-aware metrics, then run a 9,000-run causal mediation feasibility study as a verifier.

Seventeen cases (47%) look successful under logprob-only evaluation, but only one case (2.8%) passes the multimetric framework; the rest show random directions beating selected features or feature-selection collapse across PII types. The causal verifier separates candidates reliably, yet correlation-selected candidates rarely pass it. Takeaway: never accept an SAE steering or suppression claim on logprob drop alone—require matched random-direction controls and a causal mediation check. Caveat: focused on PII suppression; transfer to other SAE interventions is argued but not quantified in the abstract.

papers.title: Persona Perspectives: Adopting Viewpoints Reorganizes Representations in LLMs
papers.tldr: Prompting liberal versus conservative personas systematically shifts word projections on over 9,000 words and 33 semantic axes, and linear probes, SAE classifiers, and word-based classifiers trained without a persona then give politically slanted truthfulness and morality ratings under persona conditioning.
summary: Linear probes and sparse autoencoders usually assume that monitored features keep a stable geometry across contexts. LLMs can adopt personas that may rearrange conceptual relations, which would undermine those monitors.

The authors extract representations of over 9,000 common words and 33 semantic axes under liberal and conservative political personas and compare them to two neutral baselines, then apply persona-free linear probes, SAE-based classifiers, and manually selected word-representation classifiers to truthfulness and morality judgments on controversial statements.

Persona conditioning systematically alters word-to-axis projections and alignments among axes in directions consistent with the stated ideology, and the three monitoring methods produce divergent, politically slanted ratings of truth and morality once a persona is applied. The abstract reports no numeric deltas. Takeaway: before trusting SAE or probe monitors for safety-relevant features, test them under persona (and other context) shifts; a feature that is clean in a neutral run can reorganize under a role prompt. Caveat: only two political personas and unspecified base models in the abstract.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
papers.source: arXiv cs.CL, accepted at AACL-IJCNLP 2026 Workshop Multi-LLL (per arXiv comment)
papers.tldr: Mean-SVD and DiffPCA language subspaces capture translation-associated variation, but projecting them out leaves linear probes still nearly perfect at identifying language. On Qwen2.5-7B, the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy hurts response-language fidelity; only one setup raises joint correct-and-in-target-language accuracy, by 1.60 points.
summary: Language-subspace interventions try to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations, but it is unclear what those subspaces actually capture, whether projecting them out removes language information, and whether accuracy gains preserve the response language.

Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, the authors build Mean-SVD and DiffPCA subspaces, train linear probes on projected activations, and evaluate several intervention operators on Qwen2.5-7B while tracking both answer accuracy and response-language fidelity.

Both constructions capture substantial translation-associated variation with similar depth patterns, yet probes still identify language almost perfectly after projection, so neither subspace exhausts language information. The accuracy-best intervention sacrifices response-language fidelity; only one configuration improves joint accuracy (correct and in the target language), by 1.60 points, and prompt changes alone can reproduce accuracy gains while damaging language fidelity. Takeaway: score steering interventions on joint task-and-constraint metrics, not accuracy alone, and treat residual probeability after projection as a required check. Caveat: workshop paper; detailed per-model numbers beyond the 1.60-point joint gain are not in the abstract.

papers.title: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models
papers.tldr: Uses forced numerical choice (every integer 1–30 is valid) as a controlled setting for preference circuits: in a Qwen3-4B case a pre-answer edit flips 17 to 15, and holding later MLP outputs cuts the log-odds effect gap between two attention replacements from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat.
summary: When a language model picks a number in a range where every integer is valid, any systematic preference is a pure internal bias rather than a correctness constraint. That makes numerical choice a clean testbed for how preference is processed across layers and tokens.

Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, a pre-answer edit changes 17 to 15 while both runs first emit 1; selective cache and attention-output replacements then trace lingering influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output versus the other heads jointly restores 17 with different final log-odds on 7 versus 5; holding later MLP outputs at the edited-run values shrinks that effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts and prompt tests further separate influence from answer switches.

Later computation reshapes how similar local contributions affect the continuation, and retrospective estimates capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch; only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test, where joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap while the answer stays 17. Takeaway: for circuit-style steering studies, measure both immediate readout and downstream MLP conditioning—matched local contributions can diverge after later layers. Caveat: focused case studies on Qwen3-4B and numerical preference; authors state they do not claim a complete circuit of natural numerical preference.
